question: For the “integration-playground” provisioning project, what must a compliant implementation create, secure, automate, and prove end to end across Jira, Confluence, Slack, guest access, the GitHub webhook, lifecycle expiry, and auditability before it meets acceptance?
reference_answer: The implementation must accept team_short, owner_emails, repo_url, and expiry_days (default 14) after one Jira approval; create the INTGPLAY Kanban project with Task, Bug, and Experiment issue types plus integration, infra, and ci-cd components; clone the required Confluence template; and create a private #intg-play- Slack channel whose membership mirrors Jira roles. It must use a dedicated least-privilege service account, rotate keys every 30 days, keep webhook secrets in Vault/KMS, run from a restricted runner, and prohibit anonymous or public permissions. Guests require two owner approvals through the Slack-to-Jira flow. Creation and expiry actions must be idempotent, auditable, and sent to the central audit stream. Acceptance requires a working webhook test payload, successful end-to-end guest approval, owner notification 72 hours before expiry, and archival of Jira, Confluence, and Slack at expiry, with one extension allowed per archive cycle.

gold_evidence.evidence: requested_items: Jira project: key INTGPLAY, project template = Software Project (Kanban) with issue types: Task, Bug, Experiment. Default components: integration, infra, ci-cd. Confluence space: 'Integration Playground - INTGPLAY' cloned from a thin template that includes: incident playbook, runbook checklist, onboarding steps, and a 'CI webhook manifest' page. Slack channel: private channel #intg-play- created automatically during provisioning, members synced from Jira project roles; naming convention enforced. Service account: 'svc-intg-play-bot' with scoped tokens for Slack app and a GitHub webhook user (rotated monthly). Automation: on-create hooks that wire a repo webhook to the Confluence CI webhook manifest, and add an issue automation rule to create a runbook page when a 'Release Test' issue is transitioned. Guest approval flow: external guests require approval from two project owners via an automated request; approval should appear as a Slack message with Approve/Decline buttons that link to Jira request. Lifecycle policy: default expiry 14 days; channel/space/project archived at expiry and owners emailed 72h before; owners can extend once per archive cycle. Observability: create a lightweight audit log entry (Confluence page link) summarizing provisioning params and the GitHub repo receiving the webhook. RBAC: Project role mappings: Owners (can add guests), Members, Read-only observers; Slack members mapped to Jira roles; Confluence restrictions mirroring Jira project roles.

1. Provisioning script must use existing org templates and run with a single approval in Jira. 2) Create a GitHub webhook using a scoped service account and store the webhook secret in the vault. 3) Slack channel creation via Slack provisioning bot with membership synced from Jira project role groups. 4) Add scheduled job that checks for expired projects/spaces/channels and triggers archive workflow plus notification email. 5) All actions must be idempotent and provide human-readable audit output (timestamp, actor, params).

- Webhook secrets must be stored in Vault/KMS; never placed in Confluence pages.
- Service account keys rotated automatically and usage logged.
- Provisioning job must run in a restricted runner and require token with narrow scope.
- Audit events for create/archive must flow to central audit stream (link logs to observability pipeline).

acceptance_criteria: A templated Jira project INTGPLAY can be provisioned via the internal UI or automation script with parameters for team name and expiry. Confluence space is created from template and contains runbook and CI webhook manifest page with placeholder fields filled from provisioning parameters. Slack private channel is created with correct name and membership, and visible in Slack for all members. Approval flow for guests functions end-to-end (request -> 2 approvals -> guest added). A GitHub webhook is successfully created against a specified repo and triggers a test payload that creates an entry on the Confluence CI webhook page (test harness). Expiry job archives the Jira project, Confluence space, and Slack channel and sends owner notifications 72h prior.

question: Under “Modernize CI by replacing legacy bash pipelines with composite actions and plugin hooks,” what constraints must a repository migration and staged rollout satisfy, including supported building blocks, opt-in controls, Docker-dependent exceptions, cache and matrix safeguards, compatibility window, validation gates, and rollback?
reference_answer: The migration must add the checkout, test-shard, and lint-runner composite actions; replace shell orchestration with composite calls and the dynamic matrix generator; use ci-toolbox for cache keys and retries; remove legacy script invocations and default in-repository Docker-in-Docker usage in favor of buildah or kind; and expose staged adoption through .github/ci-config.yml. The new and legacy workflows must coexist during a two-week backward-compatible canary, with per-repository opt-in and a simple rollback to the legacy workflow reference. Repositories that still require Docker-in-Docker may set allow_dind, which defaults to false, and can configure canary_percentage. Cache keys must be previewable in dry-run mode, concurrency must be capped with dynamic shard sizing, matrix edge cases must be tested, and merge is gated on green CI and updated documentation.

gold_evidence.evidence: description: Motivation: The monolithic bash pipelines under .github/workflows and scripts/legacy-ci.sh have become brittle and hard to iterate on across services. This PR modernizes the pipeline by introducing reusable GitHub composite actions, a plugin hook system for per-repo policy, and a small cross-platform ci-toolbox binary to compute robust cache keys and talk to the remote cache store. Scope: 1) Add .github/actions/checkout-composite, test-shard-composite, lint-runner-composite. 2) Replace repo-level shell orchestration with composite action calls and a dynamic matrix generator (tools/ci/matrix-gen.js). 3) Remove scripts/legacy-ci.sh and in-repo Docker-in-Docker usage; use buildah/kind where needed. 4) Add ci-toolbox (tools/ci-toolbox/main.go) used by composite actions for cache keying and fast retries. 5) Add .github/ci-config.yml with opt-in staged rollout flags for teams to adopt incrementally. Checklist: - [x] Add composite actions and document inputs/outputs - [x] Implement matrix generator and update matrix shapes - [x] Port lint/test usages to new composites - [x] Add ci-toolbox with basic cache key and remote fetch - [x] Add integration CI job that runs composites end-to-end on a canary subset - [x] Remove legacy script invocations and update README-ci.md Migration notes: The new composites are backward-compatible by default and live alongside legacy workflows during a 2-week canary. Owners can enable ci-config.yml flags to opt into new flows. Rollback is as simple as switching the workflow reference back to legacy scripts if an issue is detected. Risks and mitigations: Cache-key changes may cause cache misses on first runs; ci-toolbox includes a dry-run mode to preview keys. Matrix reshaping can increase pipeline concurrency; we added a default concurrency limit and a dynamic shard sizing heuristic.

Evan Liu: CI runs flaked once on macOS runners in step 'install-tools' — reworked tool install order and pinned go:1.20 image in composite; reran and green. Maya Chen: Approving pending green CI and docs update. Diego Ramos: Approved. Squash-merge when ready.

question: For “Cross-SDK: unify streaming handshake, consumer ergonomics, and auth/retry semantics (Python/TS/Go),” what common contract and language-specific behavior must be implemented for stream startup and reconnect, consumption, token refresh and retries, old-server compatibility, backpressure, and cancellation?
reference_answer: All three SDKs must use CLIENT_HELLO → AUTH_OK → SERVER_READY for stream starts and reconnects, while detecting servers that omit AUTH_OK and falling back to legacy behavior with one warning per process. Python must provide StreamConsumer as an AsyncIterator and context manager with buffer_size and heartbeat_ack; TypeScript must provide createStreamConsumer callbacks plus an async iterable and backpressure controls; Go must provide NewStreamReader(ctx), reader-like single-message semantics, and clean cancellation. RetryWithAuthRefresh must use jittered exponential retries, invoke token refresh once per logical request, single-flight concurrent refreshes per token_id, and guard non-idempotent unary requests from duplicates. The default buffer size is 16, and tests must cover handshake transitions, mid-stream expiry, and cancellation without leaked goroutines.

gold_evidence.evidence:
- Introduce a lightweight stream handshake: CLIENT_HELLO -> AUTH_OK -> SERVER_READY. Implemented in each SDK with shared semantics and compatibility fallbacks for older servers.
- Consumer ergonomics: new thin abstraction that replaces ad-hoc iterators/callbacks. Python exposes StreamConsumer (AsyncIterator + context manager) with buffer_size and heartbeat_ack semantics; TS exposes createStreamConsumer({onMessage, onComplete, bufferSize}) and an async iterable wrapper; Go exposes StreamReader(ctx) that implements io.Reader-like semantics for single-message reads and a Cancel() helper.
- Auth/retries: unified RetryWithAuthRefresh policy across SDKs. Retries are jittered exponential with token refresh hook invoked once per logical request; transparent idempotency guard added for non-idempotent unary calls.
- Backwards compatibility: consumers detect old handshake flows and fall back to legacy behavior for servers that do not return AUTH_OK. Migration warnings are surfaced at runtime (single warn log per process).
- Tests: added unit tests for handshake transitions and integration e2e stream tests in a local harness that simulates mid-stream token expiration.

Migration notes:

- Python: replace raw async for msg in client.stream() with: async with client.stream_consumer() as c: async for msg in c: ...; short-lived code paths still supported but deprecated.
- TS: prefer createStreamConsumer over stream().iterator() when you need backpressure controls.
- Go: use NewStreamReader(ctx) to ensure reads cancel cleanly on token refresh.

review_comments: Raj: Can we avoid a second token refresh race if two concurrent streams call the hook? Suggest ensuring the hook is single-flight per token_id. Response: implemented singleflight guard in shared retry_policy with metrics (auth_refresh_locks). Elena: TS consumer ergonomics look good but question on buffer default. Response: default buffer_size changed to 16 and documented rationale (latency vs memory). Samir: Go Cancel() semantics — will it leak goroutines when Cancel is called mid-read? Response: added explicit test and closed goroutine via consistent context cancellation path; verified in go race run.

question: In “Copperfield Nimbus Solutions — Dedicated sizing + security notes” as of 2026-03-18, what security, networking, audit-log, legal, and commercial-readiness constraints must Redwood satisfy before the Dedicated deal can advance, and which dated next actions address the outstanding blockers?
reference_answer: Hard requirements are SAML SSO for the admin portal, a SOC 2 report, 13-month audit-log retention, KMS integration with customer-managed keys preferred, US-only data residency, and VPC deployment with peering. SCIM is a non-blocking nice-to-have, while the DPA and subprocessors list must be supplied early in legal review. Networking requires a scheduled peering window, the customer’s fixed CIDR reservation, and confirmation of MTU and routing rules. Audit logs should contain admin actions and invocation metadata—request ID, timestamps, and organization/project ID—but exclude raw prompts and responses by default. Pricing must separate chat/completion and embedding tokens, committed throughput and burst pricing, and base-versus-burst monthly ranges. Remaining blockers are customer finance approval, legal timing, final production token mix, and agreement on acceptable p95 and its measurement method. Priya’s security package is due March 19, Diego’s sizing v2 March 20, the pricing worksheet March 22, and the peering window targets the week of March 24; the POC must also demonstrate burst autoscaling and medium-to-small fallback routing.

reference_answer: The manager must publish and apply the role-specific promotion rubric and assemble an updated competency self-assessment, 360 feedback collected with the People Ops template, and evidence of impact such as PRs, release notes, or customer outcomes. Evaluation must cover increased scope beyond the current team, technical or functional depth and tradeoffs, influence through mentorship and cross-team or product leadership, and consistent contributions over 6–12 months. Final sign-off involves the manager, peer review, and the People Ops calibration committee.

question: When the automatic capacity trigger fires under the current “GPU Warm-Pool Cross-Account Handoff Runbook (2025),” what sequence and guardrails must the oncall follow from preflight through route activation and verification, including the required response to IAM failure or a stalled seed transfer?
reference_answer: The automatic path requires both p90 queue time above 2.0 seconds for three minutes and warm-pool saturation above 95% for three minutes. The oncall must confirm tenant, region, and SLO impact; check the 450 ms p99 token-serving and sub-1.0-second p95 queue-time targets; verify leases, available GPUs, preheat success, allocation-controller errors, and router-admin latency; then notify #infra-oncall and page GPU Fleet at P2 with scope and capacity metrics. IAM must be tested with redwood/gpu-warm-pool-handoff, falling back to the legacy role only if needed; if both fail, escalate and stop. Issue a single-use 120-second token and record its ID and TTL, then reserve predicted peak plus 15%. Transfer the seed with gpuctl over verified mTLS while monitoring transfer and egress metrics. If transfer stalls beyond 150 seconds, reduce to four shards and retry once; repeated failure requires aborting to DNS fallback. Activate the lease, apply a 30-minute router-admin override, and use the legacy API only where router-admin is unavailable. Verify the target pool in the last 100 request headers, confirm token_id cost attribution, and observe ten minutes of SLO data with at least a 40% queue-time reduction. Tokens must never enter external channels, and the routing override must carry an incident ticket ID.

gold_evidence.evidence:
When to run this

- Automatic trigger: capacity-sentry signals BOTH:
  - sustained 90th-percentile queue time > 2.0s for 3 minutes (was 2.5s)
  - warm-pool saturation > 95% for 3 minutes
- Manual trigger: customer-facing latency incidents, region impairment, or when the allocation controller requests cross-account burst.

Preflight (5 minutes)

1. Confirm incident context and scope: affected tenant(s), region(s), and SLO impact.
2. Check SLO dashboard (tenant-specific):
  - 99th-pct latency target: 450ms token-serving (was 500ms)
  - Queue-time SLO: 95th-pct < 1.0s (was 1.2s)
3. Verify warm-pool health in both accounts: check warm-pool-manager metrics for:
  - active leases
  - available GPUs
  - preheat success rate
4. Confirm this is not a control-plane issue:
  - allocation-controller error rate
  - router-admin config push latency

Step 0 — Notify stakeholders (2 minutes)

- Announce on #infra-oncall and page the GPU Fleet oncall (PagerDuty) with priority P2.
- Include region, tenant(s), current queue time, warm-pool saturation, and whether this is multi-region.

Step 1 — Confirm IAM and trust boundary (3 minutes)

- Validate the target account has the cross-account role configured.
  - Preferred role name: "redwood/gpu-warm-pool-handoff"
  - Legacy role name (some accounts only): "redwood/warm-pool-handoff"
- Quick check (from source account): aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::TARGET_ACCOUNT_ID:role/redwood/gpu-warm-pool-handoff --role-session-name handoff-check
- If assume-role fails:
  1. retry with legacy role name
  2. if still failing, escalate to cloud-accounts team (Slack: #cloud-accounts, oncall: @cloud-accounts). Do not proceed.

Step 2 — Issue ephemeral handshake token (1 minute)

- From burst-orchestrator console: POST /api/v1/handshake {"source_account":"A","target_account":"B","ttl_s":120}
- Record token id and TTL in the incident timeline.

Step 3 — Reserve capacity in target pool (3 minutes)

- In target account run one of the following (prefer gpuctl): kubectl -n infra exec deploy/warm-pool-manager -- /bin/gpuctl reserve --token <TOKEN_ID> --count <n_gpus>
- Sizing guidance:
  - Reserve predicted peak + 15% (was 10–20% above predicted peak); avoid over-reserving during partial incidents.

Step 4 — Seed transfer and KV-cache sync (6–12 minutes)

- Initiate transfer from source warm-pool-manager: /usr/local/bin/gpuctl transfer-seed --token <TOKEN_ID> --target-endpoint https://lease-daemon.target.internal:8443 --profile fast
- Watch transfer metrics in Prometheus:
  - warm_seed_transfer_duration_seconds
  - warm_seed_transfer_error_count
  - xnet_egress_bandwidth_utilization
- Expected durations:
  - 90% < 75s for a 4GB seed over inter-region link (with compression enabled)
- If transfer stalls > 150s (was 180s):
  1. reduce concurrent shards (--shards 4)
  2. retry once
  3. if repeated failures, abort and fall back to DNS-level routing (see Fallback options).

Step 5 — Activate lease and switch routing (2–4 minutes)

- On target: kubectl -n infra exec deploy/warm-pool-manager -- /bin/gpuctl activate --token <TOKEN_ID>
- Apply router override via router-admin (preferred): router-admin override set --tenant TENANT_ID --pool target-account-pool --ttl 30m
- Legacy (only if router-admin is unavailable in the region): POST /router/configs/apply with route override: route { tenant: "TENANT_ID", pool: "target-account-pool" }
- Wait for propagation:
  - typical: 60–90 seconds
  - if propagation exceeds 3 minutes, check router-admin backlog and config push error rate.

Verification (5 minutes)

- Confirm incoming requests are served from target pool:
  - sample last 100 requests and confirm trace header x-redwood-pool indicates target pool
- Confirm token billing tags and cost attribution are set:
  - check cost-annotator logs for token_id tag
- SLO check:
  - observe latency and queue-time dashboards for the affected tenant for a 10-minute window
  - expect queue-time to drop by >= 40% after routing changes stabilize

Security considerations

- Handshake tokens are single-use and TTL-limited (default 120s). Never paste tokens into external channels.
- All cross-account transfers must happen over mTLS endpoints; confirm certificate fingerprint before starting (see cert-check below).
- Do not run routing overrides without an incident ticket id in the override description/annotation.

question: For an existing Dedicated tenant adopting Redwood Optimize 1.3, what complete enablement and migration checklist should be followed for Performance Profiles and cost estimation, including captured data, estimator contract, compatibility changes, rollout timing, observability targets, and known fallbacks?
reference_answer: Enable optimize.performance_profiles through the Console and accept profile-generation data sharing, or generate profiles through the API or CLI. Profiles must record sequence length, generated tokens, request rate, prefix-cache hit rate, p50/p95 latency, and per-token GPU time across short, medium, and long buckets; they are versioned in the customer namespace. Cost estimates take a time window (30 days by default), models, deployment mode, commitment tier, and sequence histogram, and return monthly USD projections, input/system/output token breakdowns, and +10%, +25%, and +50% sensitivity scenarios. Cold or sparse telemetry uses conservative defaults. Existing code must rename estimate() to async estimate_cost(), remove optimize.legacy_hint to avoid HTTP 400, and handle v1-to-v2 profile conversion by re-exporting after the best-effort import. The CLI can export scheduler-ready YAML. Rollout was a ten-tenant canary on February 18, new-tenant and opt-in availability on February 20, and legacy_hint enforcement on March 10. Targets are 99.9% API availability, 99% of cached estimates within two seconds, and 95% of uncached estimates within five seconds, monitored by the three named Optimize metrics. For strict-region S3 import failures, use local CLI export/import; conservative cold-telemetry estimates remain a documented limitation.

gold_evidence.evidence:
1. Performance Profiles
  - Description: Profiles record observed stat distributions for: sequence_length, tokens_generated, request_rate (qps), prefix_cache_hit_rate. Each profile stores measured p50/p95 latencies and per-token GPU time across representative buckets (short/medium/long).
  - Storage: profiles are stored in the customer namespace (s3-backed), versioned, and visible via Console and API.
2. Telemetry-based Cost Estimator
  - Inputs: time window (default 30d), model(s), deployment mode (hosted/dedicated), commitment tier, sequence-length histogram.
  - Output: month-over-month projection (USD), token breakdown (input/system/output), sensitivity table (how cost changes if average tokens/request increases by +10/25/50%).
  - Accuracy caveats: estimator factors in measured batching efficiency and prefix cache hit rate; for cold-start or sparse telemetry customers, the estimator uses conservative defaults (see config below).

Migration notes and breaking changes

- Deprecated field removed: optimize.legacy_hint (previously used for heuristic-only recommendations). Action: remove any usages in saved route configs. Failure to remove will return 400 in API calls that include the field.
- SDK rename: update code references estimate() -> estimate_cost(). Simple search-and-replace sufficient for most codebases.
- Profile format changes: profile v1 -> v2 adds buckets for "prefix_cache_hit_rate". Dedicated scheduler accepts both v1 and v2, but v1 profiles will be automatically converted on import with a best-effort fill (read-only). We recommend re-exporting profiles after conversion.

Rollout plan

- Canary: 2026-02-18 -> enable Performance Profiles for 10 pilot tenants (selection criteria: medium-sized Dedicated customers with diverse request shapes). Monitor p95 latency impact and console correctness.
- Gradual rollout: 2026-02-20 -> enable for new tenants and opt-in for existing tenants via Console.
- Full enforcement: 2026-03-10 -> deprecate legacy_hint on route configs (400 returned if present).

SLOs and observability

- Optimize service SLO unaffected: 99.9% availability for API endpoints.
- Cost estimator-specific: 99% of estimates generated within 2s for inputs with cached Performance Profiles; 95% within 5s for uncached inputs.
- Telemetry metrics exposed: optimize.profile_generation.count, optimize.estimate_latency_ms.p95, optimize.estimate_cache_hit_rate. Dashboards: /dashboards/optimize/1-3-release-estimates

How to opt-in / try it today

1. Console: Admin -> Feature flags -> toggle optimize.performance_profiles -> follow "Enable" flow to accept data-sharing for profile generation.
2. API: POST /v1/optimize/profiles?action=generate with model + window_days.
3. CLI: redwood optimize export-profile --generate redwood-7b-v1 --window 7d --out my-profile.yaml

Known issues and limitations

- Cold telemetry causes conservative cost projections (noted in UI). We plan a future release (1.4) to add synthetic workload injection to reduce conservatism.
- Some legacy Dedicated accounts with strict region restrictions may see profile import failures due to S3 path policies; workaround: use CLI export/import via local file.

question: For the NorthPoint Signalworks four-week Dedicated POC, what complete test and purchase-readiness plan was agreed across capacity and model topology, rollout and rollback, measurable success thresholds, security and network controls, commercial criteria, blockers, and next steps?
reference_answer: The POC uses a four-A100-equivalent reserved pool for 200–400 daily concurrent users, with quantized Llama-2-70B as baseline and 13B as canary and load-degradation fallback. us-east-1 is primary and eu-west-1 is the warm-standby secondary, with region failover preferred to throttling. Traffic advances 5% → 25% → 50% → 100% over four days and automatically rolls back on evaluation regression, p95 above 200 ms, or error rate above 0.5%. Formal success metrics are p95 below 180 ms for short chat, p50 below 80 ms, token cost below $0.0009, error rate below 0.5%, and acceptable autoscaling to twice baseline. Security requires SAML SSO, customer-managed KMS, twelve-month audit logs, US-only PII residency, VPC peering, an egress allowlist, stable static egress IPs, SOC 2 scope evidence, and a KMS architecture. Purchase depends on latency, security-checklist completion, and TCO; annual committed capacity is preferred if discounted 10–20%. Blockers are finance approval, peering and allowlisting, IdP details, and the data-residency addendum. Next steps are to finalize the SOW and pricing, start the SecOps infrastructure kickoff, and provide model variants, quantization/kernel guidance, and canary configuration.

gold_evidence.evidence: notes: POC objective: validate Dedicated pool for interactive chat + embeddings at mid-market scale (200-400 daily concurrent users). Latency targets: p95 <180ms for short chat (<=512 tokens); p50 <80ms. Product lead: "We can't accept >150ms 95p for primary flows" (sourced earlier). Throughput & cost: target token unit cost < $0.0009 during POC; acceptable burst behavior with autoscaling up to 2x baseline. Model strategy: baseline = Llama-2-70B quantized (fast kernels); canary variant = Llama-2-13B quantized; fallback to 13B under heavy load or degraded perf. Routing plan agreed for POC: primary region = us-east-1, secondary = eu-west-1. Failover preference = region failover (warm standby) over throttling. Canary rollout plan: 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% over 4 days. Automatic rollback triggers: quality regression (eval suite), latency breach >200ms p95, or error rate >0.5%. Security constraints: customer requires SAML SSO, customer-managed KMS for key wrapping, audit logs with 12-month retention, and US-only residency for PII flows. Networking: must complete VPC peering + egress allowlist; team flagged requirement for stable static egress IPs for compliance. Open ask: provide example quantization profiles and recommended kernel settings for customer inference budget; sample config in Drive link. Quote from CTO on call: "We like the routing/fallback idea — want clear SLAs on rollback automation and model parity metrics." Decision criteria for purchase: meets latency SLAs in POC, passes security checklist, and forecasted TCO within estimated range. Internal stakeholders: Product (Emily R), Infra Lead (David H), SecOps (Rina S), Finance (Alex P). Sales notes: pricing sensitivity — prefer annual committed capacity if 10–20% discount off list, will consider Dedicated reserved pool if SLOs match.

question: For the Kestrel Helpdesk Systems two-week POC, what complete scope and acceptance plan must be covered across source data, assistant behavior, integration surfaces, performance and quality, security, weekly execution, assigned deliverables, blockers, and the path from Hosted to Dedicated?
reference_answer: The POC must ingest six months of anonymized ticket history plus a Confluence knowledge-base export. It must deliver streaming responses and callable server-side tools for user profile, order lookup, ticket lookup, and CRM enrichment through Node and Python SDK integration and WebSocket streaming. Acceptance requires first-token latency below 1.5 seconds at p95 with a 500 ms median target, 50 concurrent agents, and relevance at least equal to the current heuristic baseline on 300 prompts. Security requires US-only residency, SAML SSO, SCIM, KMS, and twelve-month audit logs. Week 0 covers security sign-off, account creation, and sample upload; week 1 integrates streaming and tool calls and runs 1,000 synthetic conversations; week 2 shadows ten live agents, runs the 50-agent test, and produces the latency report. Jordan’s proposal is due March 18, Samir’s load-test plan and scripts March 12, and Kestrel’s anonymized data March 14. Blockers are the MSA residency clause, blended committed pricing, KMS and SOC 2 proof, and validation of the latency SLO at peak. The commercial path starts Hosted and targets Dedicated in 6–12 months if latency and unit economics work for about 30 million tokens per month.

question: For the March 13, 2026 dsp-6-us-east embeddings incident affecting NimbleSearch, what complete remediation and closure record should be reported, covering immediate containment, permanent fixes and deployment results, recovery evidence, customer communication, and preventive follow-ups?
reference_answer: Immediate containment added three dsp-6 nodes, capped NimbleSearch routine jobs at 60 RPS, restored the previous prefetch.window_size, and enabled API-gateway soft backoff to suppress hedged-retry flooding. The permanent fix bounded the runtime worker pool with better nproc fallback and changed the gateway to honor backend-capacity signals. Gateway PR #3842 deployed at 19:05Z and the runtime patch at 19:40Z; the 5xx rate returned to about 0.6% within twenty minutes, no further pthread_create failures appeared on the patched nodes, and mitigation was declared at 19:50Z. NimbleSearch was notified, accepted the temporary limit, and requested a postmortem and safe-batch guidance. Follow-ups are a worker-exhaustion runbook with thresholds, more aggressive batch-tenant autoscaler warmup, large-batch preflight and recommended sizes, region-specific prefetch rollout gates, and a pthread_create alert that auto-throttles affected tenants; the adjusted warmup policy is to be watched for 48 hours.

gold_evidence.evidence:
mitigation: Applied immediate mitigations:

- Scaled dedicated pool dsp-6 by +3 nodes to absorb burst.
- Added tenant-level temporary rate-limit to 60rps for NimbleSearch routine jobs to stop retry spin.
- Rolled back global prefetch.window_size for dsp-6 to previous value to reduce work amplification.
- Enabled apigw soft-backoff so hedged retries won't flood runtimes while autoscaler warms up.

resolution: Root cause addressed by a two-part fix: 1) runtime hardening to allocate a bounded worker thread pool (prevents unbounded pthread_create) and better nproc fallback handling, and 2) apigw change to honor backend capacity signals and avoid hedged retry amplification. Hotfix (infra PR #3842) deployed into us-east on 2026-03-13 19:05Z and runtime patch rolled on 2026-03-13 19:40Z. Post-deploy: 5xx rate dropped back to baseline ~0.6% within 20 minutes. Resolution steps recorded and communicated to NimbleSearch. Incident declared mitigated at 2026-03-13T19:50Z; full resolution pending follow-ups.

follow_up:

- Create a runbook entry for 'thread/worker pool exhaustion' and include detection thresholds.
- Adjust autoscaler warmup policy for dsp-* pools to be more aggressive for batch-heavy tenants.
- Add tenant-level preflight checks for large-batch embedding uploads with recommended batch sizes.
- Audit prefetch config rollout gating so we don't apply global prefetch increases without region-specific safety checks.
- Add metric alert to detect 'pthread_create failure' log pattern and auto-throttle affected tenants.

question: For “Migrate interaction tokens to theme variable layer and resolve hover glow regression,” what complete pre-merge coverage is required across state, variant, and theme scope, visual parity, motion and keyboard accessibility, test artifacts, documentation and design deliverables, remaining defects, and follow-up work?
reference_answer: All hover, focus, active, disabled, pressed, and loading colors and elevation effects must move from component-local tokens to theme variables for primary, secondary, ghost, destructive, link, icon-only, and compact buttons across light, dark, and high-contrast themes. Default-theme appearance must remain unchanged except for the intended glow fix, and the original defect must be reproduced before the fix and proven absent afterward. Reduced-motion mode may add no motion or double shadows. Deliverables are the token migration PR, synchronized Figma tokens and PR link, component documentation with migration rationale and troubleshooting, storyshots, Cypress/Percy visual coverage, and accessibility sign-off. QA must exercise every variant, all three themes, reduced motion, repeated loading toggles, and keyboard focus with a three-pixel visible threshold in high contrast, with all Percy diffs resolved before merge. The ghost focus regression was addressed with a high-contrast focus token and border-image thickness, but one dark-theme compact-icon case remained under investigation and blocks final merge. Follow-ups are a token-source diagnostic story, optional runtime hover debounce if extreme-load jitter persists, and an audit of table and chart interaction tokens. Button anatomy changes and JavaScript hover batching are outside this ticket’s scope.

description: Summary: Migrate all interactive state colors and elevation effects (hover, focus, active, disabled, pressed, and loading overlays) from component-local tokens into the new theme variable layer so they resolve consistently across light/dark/high-contrast themes. Deliverables: token migration PR, Figma token update, updated component docs, automated Cypress+Percy snapshots, accessibility signoff.

Out of scope: Rewriting button anatomy or changing visual language beyond aligning existing tokens to the theme; any JS runtime batching of hover events (handled by runtime team).
